name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_EQUILIBRIUM_DIAGRAM_Q01 - Measuring equilibrium vapour pressure of water

questiontext.text:
The diagram below shows two closed transparent boxes fitted with mercury U-tube manometers at a constant temperature. Box I contains anhydrous calcium chloride, while Box II contains a dish of water after the drying agent is removed.

After some time, the mercury level in the right limb of the manometer in Box II stops rising and becomes constant. What does this constant difference in mercury levels represent?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Box I contains anhydrous \(\mathrm{CaCl}_2\) (a drying agent), so the air inside is dry and both limbs of its manometer have equal mercury levels. Box II contains a dish of liquid water in a closed box at constant temperature, and the right limb of its manometer rises and reaches a constant height.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The closed box prevents any escape of water vapour to the surroundings, and temperature is held constant throughout the observation.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
In a closed container, liquid water and water vapour establish a dynamic equilibrium: \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}(\mathrm{l}) \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}(\mathrm{vap})\), where the rate of evaporation equals the rate of condensation.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
As water evaporates into the dry box, the number of vapour molecules increases, raising the total pressure inside Box II and pushing the mercury up in the right limb. Once the rate of condensation equals the rate of evaporation, there is no net change in the amount of water vapour, so the pressure stabilizes at a constant value.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The constant pressure difference recorded by the manometer at equilibrium corresponds to the equilibrium vapour pressure of water at that temperature.

answer.text: The equilibrium vapour pressure of water at that temperature
The normal boiling point of water at atmospheric pressure
The complete conversion of liquid water into vapour
The partial pressure of dry air absorbed by calcium chloride

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_EQUILIBRIUM_DIAGRAM_Q02 - Attainment of chemical equilibrium concentration graph

questiontext.text:
The graph below illustrates the variation of concentrations of reactants (\(\mathrm{A}\) or \(\mathrm{B}\)) and products (\(\mathrm{C}\) or \(\mathrm{D}\)) with time for the reversible reaction \(\mathrm{A} + \mathrm{B} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{C} + \mathrm{D}\).

Which statement accurately describes the chemical system at and beyond the vertical dashed line marked "Equilibrium"?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The graph plots concentration on the vertical axis against time on the horizontal axis for the reaction \(\mathrm{A} + \mathrm{B} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{C} + \mathrm{D}\). The reactant curve (\(\mathrm{A}\) or \(\mathrm{B}\)) starts at a high concentration and decreases, while the product curve (\(\mathrm{C}\) or \(\mathrm{D}\)) starts at zero and increases. Both curves become horizontal at the vertical dashed line.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The reaction is carried out in a closed vessel at a constant temperature.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Chemical equilibrium is dynamic in nature: at equilibrium, the rate of the forward reaction equals the rate of the reverse reaction, so there is no net change in the concentrations of reactants and products.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Before the dashed line, reactant concentrations fall and product concentrations rise, slowing the forward reaction and accelerating the reverse reaction. At the dashed line, both rates become equal, causing the concentration curves to flatten into horizontal lines without dropping to zero.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Therefore, at and beyond the equilibrium line, the forward and reverse reactions continue at equal rates and the concentrations of all species remain constant.

answer.text: Both the forward and reverse reactions have completely stopped.
The concentrations of reactants and products must be equal to each other.
The rates of the forward and reverse reactions are equal, and all concentrations remain constant.
The rate of the forward reaction continues to exceed the rate of the reverse reaction.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_EQUILIBRIUM_DIAGRAM_Q03 - Haber process ammonia synthesis concentration curves

questiontext.text:
The graph below depicts the change in molar concentrations of the species involved in the synthesis of ammonia by Haber's process: \(\mathrm{N}_2(\mathrm{g}) + 3\mathrm{H}_2(\mathrm{g}) \rightleftharpoons 2\mathrm{NH}_3(\mathrm{g})\), starting from a mixture of \(\mathrm{N}_2\) and \(\mathrm{H}_2\) in stoichiometric proportions.

Identify the species represented by Curve P, Curve Q, and Curve R, respectively.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The reaction is \(\mathrm{N}_2(\mathrm{g}) + 3\mathrm{H}_2(\mathrm{g}) \rightleftharpoons 2\mathrm{NH}_3(\mathrm{g})\). In the graph, Curve P starts at the highest molar concentration and decreases, Curve Q starts at a lower non-zero concentration and decreases less steeply, and Curve R starts at zero and increases until all three curves level off at equilibrium.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Initially only the reactants \(\mathrm{N}_2\) and \(\mathrm{H}_2\) are present in stoichiometric amounts (1:3 molar ratio), and no product \(\mathrm{NH}_3\) is present at \(t = 0\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
By reaction stoichiometry, for every \(1\;\mathrm{mol}\) of \(\mathrm{N}_2\) consumed, \(3\;\mathrm{mol}\) of \(\mathrm{H}_2\) are consumed and \(2\;\mathrm{mol}\) of \(\mathrm{NH}_3\) are formed.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Since Curve R starts at zero concentration and increases with time, it must represent the product \(\mathrm{NH}_3\). Between the two reactants, \(\mathrm{H}_2\) has three times the initial concentration and three times the drop in concentration compared to \(\mathrm{N}_2\). Therefore, the higher-concentration decreasing curve (Curve P) represents \(\mathrm{H}_2\), and the lower-concentration decreasing curve (Curve Q) represents \(\mathrm{N}_2\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Thus, Curve P is \(\mathrm{H}_2\), Curve Q is \(\mathrm{N}_2\), and Curve R is \(\mathrm{NH}_3\).

answer.text: \(\mathrm{N}_2\), \(\mathrm{H}_2\), and \(\mathrm{NH}_3\)
\(\mathrm{H}_2\), \(\mathrm{N}_2\), and \(\mathrm{NH}_3\)
\(\mathrm{NH}_3\), \(\mathrm{H}_2\), and \(\mathrm{N}_2\)
\(\mathrm{H}_2\), \(\mathrm{NH}_3\), and \(\mathrm{N}_2\)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_EQUILIBRIUM_DIAGRAM_Q04 - Attaining equilibrium from either direction in HI system

questiontext.text:
The graph below shows how the same equilibrium state is reached from either direction for the reaction \(\mathrm{H}_2(\mathrm{g}) + \mathrm{I}_2(\mathrm{g}) \rightleftharpoons 2\mathrm{HI}(\mathrm{g})\). On the left, the experiment begins with equal concentrations of \(\mathrm{H}_2\) and \(\mathrm{I}_2\); on the right, it begins with pure \(\mathrm{HI}\).

What condition must be satisfied for the two experiments to yield the exact same equilibrium concentrations of \(\mathrm{H}_2\), \(\mathrm{I}_2\), and \(\mathrm{HI}\) at the same temperature?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The graph shows two experiments at the same temperature: one starting from \(\mathrm{H}_2(\mathrm{g})\) and \(\mathrm{I}_2(\mathrm{g})\) (left to right) and the other starting from pure \(\mathrm{HI}(\mathrm{g})\) (right to left). Both meet at identical equilibrium concentrations at the central dashed line.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Both reactions take place in closed vessels of fixed volume at the same temperature.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Chemical equilibrium is independent of the direction from which it is approached, provided the elemental composition (total number of atoms of each element per unit volume) and temperature are identical.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
If the left-hand experiment starts with \(c\) moles per litre each of \(\mathrm{H}_2\) and \(\mathrm{I}_2\), it contains \(2c\) moles of \(\mathrm{H}\) atoms and \(2c\) moles of \(\mathrm{I}\) atoms per litre. For the right-hand experiment starting with pure \(\mathrm{HI}\) to reach the identical equilibrium concentrations, it must start with \(2c\) moles per litre of \(\mathrm{HI}\) so that the total number of \(\mathrm{H}\) and \(\mathrm{I}\) atoms in the given volume is the same.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Thus, the total number of \(\mathrm{H}\) and \(\mathrm{I}\) atoms in the given volume must be the same in both experiments.

answer.text: A catalyst must be added only to the reverse decomposition of \(\mathrm{HI}\).
The initial molar concentration of \(\mathrm{HI}\) must equal the initial concentration of \(\mathrm{H}_2\).
The initial pressure of \(\mathrm{HI}\) must be half the sum of the initial pressures of \(\mathrm{H}_2\) and \(\mathrm{I}_2\).
The total number of \(\mathrm{H}\) and \(\mathrm{I}\) atoms in the given volume must be the same in both experiments.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_EQUILIBRIUM_DIAGRAM_Q05 - Predicting reaction direction from Qc and Kc bars

questiontext.text:
The bar diagram compares the reaction quotient \(Q_c\) and the equilibrium constant \(K_c\) for a reversible reaction \(\text{Reactants} \rightleftharpoons \text{Products}\) at three different stages.

In Stage Z, where \(Q_c > K_c\), how do the reaction direction and the Gibbs energy change \(\Delta G\) for the forward reaction behave?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
In Stage Z of the bar chart, the bar for the reaction quotient \(Q_c\) is taller than the bar for the equilibrium constant \(K_c\), meaning \(Q_c > K_c\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Temperature \(T\) is constant, and \(\Delta G\) refers to the Gibbs energy change for the forward reaction as written (\(\text{Reactants} \rightarrow \text{Products}\)).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
The thermodynamic relation between \(\Delta G\), \(Q\), and \(K\) is \(\Delta G = \Delta G^\circ + RT\ln Q\). Since \(\Delta G^\circ = -RT\ln K\), this simplifies to \(\Delta G = RT\ln\left(\frac{Q}{K}\right)\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Because \(Q_c > K_c\), the ratio \(\frac{Q_c}{K_c} > 1\), which makes \(\ln\left(\frac{Q_c}{K_c}\right) > 0\). Therefore, \(\Delta G > 0\) for the forward reaction, meaning the forward reaction is non-spontaneous and the net reaction proceeds spontaneously in the reverse direction (from products to reactants) until \(Q_c = K_c\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Thus, in Stage Z, \(\Delta G > 0\) for the forward reaction and the net reaction proceeds from products to reactants.

answer.text: Net reaction proceeds from products to reactants, and \(\Delta G > 0\) for the forward reaction.
Net reaction proceeds from reactants to products, and \(\Delta G < 0\) for the forward reaction.
No net reaction occurs, and \(\Delta G = 0\) for the forward reaction.
Net reaction proceeds from products to reactants, and \(\Delta G < 0\) for the forward reaction.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_EQUILIBRIUM_DIAGRAM_Q06 - Effect of adding hydrogen to HI equilibrium

questiontext.text:
The graph below shows the effect of adding \(\mathrm{H}_2\) gas at time \(t_1\) to an equilibrium mixture of \(\mathrm{H}_2(\mathrm{g}) + \mathrm{I}_2(\mathrm{g}) \rightleftharpoons 2\mathrm{HI}(\mathrm{g})\) at constant temperature and volume, until a new equilibrium is re-established at time \(t_2\).

Comparing the concentrations at the newly established equilibrium (\(t_2\)) with those at the original equilibrium (before \(t_1\)), which statement is true?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
At time \(t_1\), \(\mathrm{H}_2\) is added instantaneously to the equilibrium mixture \(\mathrm{H}_2(\mathrm{g}) + \mathrm{I}_2(\mathrm{g}) \rightleftharpoons 2\mathrm{HI}(\mathrm{g})\), causing a sharp upward spike in \([\mathrm{H}_2]\). Between \(t_1\) and \(t_2\), \([\mathrm{H}_2]\) and \([\mathrm{I}_2]\) decrease while \([\mathrm{HI}]\) increases until plateauing at \(t_2\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Temperature and volume remain constant, so \(K_c\) does not change.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
By Le Chatelier's principle, adding a reactant shifts the equilibrium in the forward direction to partially consume the added substance. In terms of the reaction quotient, \(Q_c = \frac{[\mathrm{HI}]^2}{[\mathrm{H}_2][\mathrm{I}_2]} < K_c\) immediately after adding \(\mathrm{H}_2\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
As the reaction shifts forward, \(\mathrm{I}_2\) is consumed along with some of the added \(\mathrm{H}_2\), producing more \(\mathrm{HI}\). Therefore, at \(t_2\), \([\mathrm{HI}]\) is higher and \([\mathrm{I}_2]\) is lower than before \(t_1\). Meanwhile, \([\mathrm{H}_2]\) decreases from its spike at \(t_1\) but remains higher than its original equilibrium value before \(t_1\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Hence, at \(t_2\), \([\mathrm{H}_2]\) and \([\mathrm{HI}]\) are higher than before \(t_1\), while \([\mathrm{I}_2]\) is lower than before \(t_1\).

answer.text: \([\mathrm{H}_2]\) returns to its exact value before \(t_1\), while \([\mathrm{HI}]\) increases.
\([\mathrm{H}_2]\), \([\mathrm{I}_2]\), and \([\mathrm{HI}]\) are all higher at \(t_2\) than before \(t_1\).
\([\mathrm{H}_2]\) and \([\mathrm{HI}]\) are higher than before \(t_1\), while \([\mathrm{I}_2]\) is lower than before \(t_1\).
\([\mathrm{I}_2]\) and \([\mathrm{HI}]\) both decrease between \(t_1\) and \(t_2\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_EQUILIBRIUM_DIAGRAM_Q07 - Predicting extent of reaction from Kc scale

questiontext.text:
The scale below shows the dependence of the extent of a chemical reaction on the magnitude of its equilibrium constant \(K_c\).

For the dissociation \(\mathrm{N}_2\mathrm{O}_4(\mathrm{g}) \rightleftharpoons 2\mathrm{NO}_2(\mathrm{g})\) at \(25^\circ\mathrm{C}\), \(K_c = 4.64 \times 10^{-3}\). Based on this scale, which description applies to the equilibrium mixture?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
For \(\mathrm{N}_2\mathrm{O}_4(\mathrm{g}) \rightleftharpoons 2\mathrm{NO}_2(\mathrm{g})\) at \(25^\circ\mathrm{C}\), \(K_c = 4.64 \times 10^{-3}\). On the scale, the central region spans from \(10^{-3}\) to \(10^3\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The equilibrium mixture is contained in a closed vessel at \(25^\circ\mathrm{C}\).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
The magnitude of \(K_c\) indicates the relative amounts of products and reactants at equilibrium: if \(K_c > 10^3\), products predominate; if \(K_c < 10^{-3}\), reactants predominate; and if \(10^{-3} \le K_c \le 10^3\), neither strongly predominates.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Since \(4.64 \times 10^{-3} > 10^{-3}\) and \(4.64 \times 10^{-3} < 10^3\), the value of \(K_c\) lies in the intermediate range between \(10^{-3}\) and \(10^3\). Consequently, both \(\mathrm{N}_2\mathrm{O}_4\) and \(\mathrm{NO}_2\) are present in appreciable concentrations at equilibrium.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Therefore, appreciable concentrations of both reactants and products are present at equilibrium.

answer.text: The reaction proceeds nearly to completion with negligible \(\mathrm{N}_2\mathrm{O}_4\) remaining.
Appreciable concentrations of both \(\mathrm{N}_2\mathrm{O}_4\) and \(\mathrm{NO}_2\) are present at equilibrium.
The reaction hardly proceeds, leaving almost pure \(\mathrm{N}_2\mathrm{O}_4\) with undetectable \(\mathrm{NO}_2\).
The reaction reaches equilibrium instantaneously because \(K_c\) is close to \(10^{-3}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_EQUILIBRIUM_DIAGRAM_Q08 - Effect of temperature on NO2 N2O4 equilibrium

questiontext.text:
Three sealed test tubes containing an identical equilibrium mixture of brown \(\mathrm{NO}_2(\mathrm{g})\) and colourless \(\mathrm{N}_2\mathrm{O}_4(\mathrm{g})\), governed by \(2\mathrm{NO}_2(\mathrm{g}) \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{N}_2\mathrm{O}_4(\mathrm{g})\;\; (\Delta H = -57.2\;\mathrm{kJ\;mol}^{-1})\), are placed in three beakers at different temperatures as shown below.

Which explanation correctly accounts for the deepest brown colour observed in the \(363\;\mathrm{K}\) beaker?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The equilibrium is \(2\mathrm{NO}_2(\mathrm{g}) \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{N}_2\mathrm{O}_4(\mathrm{g})\) with \(\Delta H = -57.2\;\mathrm{kJ\;mol}^{-1}\). \(\mathrm{NO}_2\) is brown, whereas \(\mathrm{N}_2\mathrm{O}_4\) is colourless. The three sealed tubes are at \(270\;\mathrm{K}\), \(298\;\mathrm{K}\), and \(363\;\mathrm{K}\), with the \(363\;\mathrm{K}\) tube showing the darkest brown colour.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
A negative \(\Delta H\) indicates that the forward dimerization reaction is exothermic, while the reverse dissociation reaction is endothermic.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
According to Le Chatelier's principle and the temperature dependence of equilibrium constants, increasing the temperature of an exothermic reaction decreases \(K_c\) and shifts the equilibrium in the endothermic (reverse) direction.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
At \(363\;\mathrm{K}\), the higher temperature favours the endothermic reverse reaction \(\mathrm{N}_2\mathrm{O}_4(\mathrm{g}) \rightarrow 2\mathrm{NO}_2(\mathrm{g})\). This decreases \(K_c\) and increases the equilibrium concentration of brown \(\mathrm{NO}_2\) gas, intensifying the brown colour.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Conversely, at \(270\;\mathrm{K}\) the exothermic forward reaction is favoured, producing more colourless \(\mathrm{N}_2\mathrm{O}_4\) and a paler colour. Thus, the deepest brown colour at \(363\;\mathrm{K}\) occurs because raising the temperature decreases \(K_c\) for the exothermic forward reaction and shifts the equilibrium toward \(\mathrm{NO}_2\).

answer.text: Dimerization of \(\mathrm{NO}_2\) is endothermic, so heating increases \(K_c\) and forms more \(\mathrm{N}_2\mathrm{O}_4\).
Increasing temperature increases the total pressure in the sealed tube, shifting the equilibrium toward \(\mathrm{NO}_2\) without changing \(K_c\).
Higher temperature increases the rate of the forward reaction more than the reverse reaction, forming more \(\mathrm{NO}_2\).
Dimerization of \(\mathrm{NO}_2\) is exothermic, so raising the temperature decreases \(K_c\) and shifts the equilibrium toward \(\mathrm{NO}_2\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_EQUILIBRIUM_DIAGRAM_Q09 - Structure and hydration of hydronium ion

questiontext.text:
The diagram below represents the hydrated hydronium ion species \(\mathrm{H}_9\mathrm{O}_4^+\) formed when a proton dissolves in aqueous solution.

What is the geometry of the central \(\mathrm{H}_3\mathrm{O}^+\) unit in this structure, and why cannot a bare \(\mathrm{H}^+\) ion exist freely in aqueous solution?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The diagram shows a central \(\mathrm{H}_3\mathrm{O}^+\) ion covalently bonded to three \(\mathrm{H}\) atoms, each of which forms a hydrogen bond (dashed line) to a surrounding \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\) molecule, giving \(\mathrm{H}_9\mathrm{O}_4^+\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The central oxygen atom in \(\mathrm{H}_3\mathrm{O}^+\) has three \(\mathrm{O}-\mathrm{H}\) covalent bonds and one remaining lone pair of electrons.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
According to Arrhenius and Brönsted-Lowry concepts, a bare proton \(\mathrm{H}^+\) has a radius of approximately \(10^{-15}\;\mathrm{m}\) and produces an intense electric field.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Because of its tiny size and intense electric field, a bare proton cannot exist freely in water; it immediately binds to one of the two lone pairs on a solvent \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\) molecule to form \(\mathrm{H}_3\mathrm{O}^+\). With three bond pairs and one lone pair around the central oxygen atom, \(\mathrm{H}_3\mathrm{O}^+\) adopts a trigonal pyramidal geometry, and it is further hydrated via hydrogen bonding to give species like \(\mathrm{H}_5\mathrm{O}_2^+\), \(\mathrm{H}_7\mathrm{O}_3^+\), and \(\mathrm{H}_9\mathrm{O}_4^+\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Thus, the \(\mathrm{H}_3\mathrm{O}^+\) unit has a trigonal pyramidal geometry, and \(\mathrm{H}^+\) cannot exist freely because its extremely small size and intense electric field cause it to bind to a lone pair on a water molecule.

answer.text: Trigonal pyramidal; a bare proton has a very small radius (\(\sim 10^{-15}\;\mathrm{m}\)) and intense electric field, so it binds to a lone pair on \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\).
Trigonal planar; a bare proton transfers an electron to \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\) to form a neutral radical.
Tetrahedral; a bare proton accepts two lone pairs simultaneously from a single \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\) molecule.
Linear; a bare proton has a large ionic radius and repels surrounding water dipoles.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_EQUILIBRIUM_DIAGRAM_Q10 - Dual Bronsted Lowry role of water

questiontext.text:
The two proton-transfer schematics below illustrate the reactions of \(\mathrm{NH}_3\) and \(\mathrm{HCl}\) with water in aqueous solution.

Based on these schematics, which statement correctly identifies the Brönsted-Lowry role of \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\) and its conjugate partner in each reaction?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Reaction I shows \(\mathrm{NH}_3\) gaining a proton to form \(\mathrm{NH}_4^+\) while \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\) loses a proton to form \(\mathrm{OH}^-\). Reaction II shows \(\mathrm{HCl}\) losing a proton to form \(\mathrm{Cl}^-\) while \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\) gains a proton to form \(\mathrm{H}_3\mathrm{O}^+\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
According to the Brönsted-Lowry definition, an acid is a proton (\(\mathrm{H}^+\)) donor and a base is a proton acceptor. A conjugate acid-base pair differs by a single proton.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
When an acid donates \(\mathrm{H}^+\), it forms its conjugate base (one fewer proton). When a base accepts \(\mathrm{H}^+\), it forms its conjugate acid (one extra proton).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
In Reaction I, \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\) donates a proton to \(\mathrm{NH}_3\) and therefore acts as a Brönsted acid, forming its conjugate base \(\mathrm{OH}^-\). In Reaction II, \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\) accepts a proton from \(\mathrm{HCl}\) and therefore acts as a Brönsted base, forming its conjugate acid \(\mathrm{H}_3\mathrm{O}^+\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
This demonstrates the dual (amphoteric) role of water: it acts as a Brönsted acid with conjugate base \(\mathrm{OH}^-\) in Reaction I, and as a Brönsted base with conjugate acid \(\mathrm{H}_3\mathrm{O}^+\) in Reaction II.

answer.text: \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\) acts as a Brönsted base in both reactions, forming \(\mathrm{OH}^-\) in Reaction I and \(\mathrm{H}_3\mathrm{O}^+\) in Reaction II.
\(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\) acts as a Brönsted base in Reaction I (conjugate acid \(\mathrm{OH}^-\)) and as a Brönsted acid in Reaction II (conjugate base \(\mathrm{H}_3\mathrm{O}^+\)).
\(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\) acts as a Brönsted acid in Reaction I (conjugate base \(\mathrm{OH}^-\)) and as a Brönsted base in Reaction II (conjugate acid \(\mathrm{H}_3\mathrm{O}^+\)).
\(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\) acts as a Brönsted acid in both reactions because it always donates a proton in aqueous equilibria.
